EUR/USD might be bottoming out amid peak Fed hawkishness and dovish repricing risks
body: The US dollar has found support recently from a hawkish repricing in interest rate expectations following Governor Waller’s remarks, in which he even floated the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike at the December meeting. Higher-than-expected US inflation data added to the hawkish sentiment.
Moreover, the greenback benefited from safe-haven flows as global growth concerns intensified amid a more hawkish Fed, the prolonged US-Iran stalemate and a global stock market selloff.

Those same growth concerns, though, triggered a dovish repricing of Fed rate hike expectations further out the curve, as markets anticipated that the stock market rout could significantly weigh on the broader economy. This has caused the yield differential to favour the upside for the EUR/USD pair, although the greenback remained resilient thanks to safe-haven demand.
Looking ahead, we might see the US dollar coming under more pressure in case the Fed sounds less hawkish than expected or the economic data triggers a dovish repricing in interest rates expectations.

On the EUR side, the ECB is widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 bps at the December meeting and deliver one final hike in June 2027. Growth is holding up well, but the recovery remains uneven, with France being a drag. Inflation and energy-related risks are still complicating the ECB’s job of getting inflation sustainably back to target.

France's 2027 budget battle is still ongoing, and the government is struggling to get its deficit-reduction plans through parliament. So, the French fiscal story remains unresolved. The key risk for French bonds is that parliament waters down the government's consolidation measures, leaving France with a higher deficit for longer. This could keep the French-German 10-year yield spread and the euro under pressure.

At the end of the day, the EUR/USD pair is 80% driven by what happens with the US dollar, so a dovish repricing in Fed interest rate expectations will likely outweigh euro-related woes, especially given the overbought US dollar positioning.

On the daily chart, we can see that EURUSD is consolidating near recent lows as traders await new catalysts. If we get a pullback into the downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 1.08 handle. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the major downward trendline around the 1.15 handle, with the 1.1270 level as the first target.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a resistance zone around the 1.10 level. We can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the downward trendline.

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. The buyers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to pile in for a drop into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

news.title: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
body: The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.

The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.

On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.

China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."

He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.

The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.
The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.
"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.

news.title: Crude oil finds some footing as prolonged US-Iran tensions keep the downside limited. What's next?
body: Crude oil started to find some footing recently as the bearish pressure from growth concerns eased. Keep in mind that growth fears could still push oil prices lower, but we will likely need a bigger selloff in the stock market, an even more hawkish Fed or weak economic data to increase the bearish momentum.
On the news front, we had a relatively quiet day yesterday with no major developments, although we continue to have incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.

Overall, there’s been no de-escalation nor improvement in the US-Iran situation as the risk of a direct military confrontation remains high. Oil prices could come under renewed pressure if growth concerns intensify, but an escalation in the war could still push prices higher, while a prolonged stalemate may keep the downside limited.

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil (CFD contract) extended the gains yesterday after a key technical breakout on the lower timeframes. If we get another retest of the support zone around the 80.00 level, we can expect the buyers to step in there, with a defined risk below the support, to keep targeting the 110.00 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will need the price to break lower to pile in for a drop into the 68.00 support next, with the 74.00 handle as the first target.

On the 4 hour chart, we can see that the price reversed before reaching the upper bound of the channel. If we get another push to the upside, we can expect the sellers to lean on the top trendline, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 68.00 support. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the 92.50 level next.

On the 1 hour chart, we can see that the break of the downward trendline increased the bullish momentum as more buyers piled in to target the upper bound of the channel. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to lean on the upward trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

news.title: Gold remains caught between forced liquidations and hawkish Fed bets. What could trigger a reversal?
body: Gold probed briefly below the key 3,500 level yesterday before rebounding strongly and erasing most of the weekly losses.

The price action has become choppy across many markets as traders await new catalysts to pick a direction. The US holiday today doesn’t help either, as thinner liquidity could lead to random price swings.

For gold, it’s a tricky situation because it keeps getting smashed lower on forced liquidations when the stock market falls and the gains are capped when the sentiment improves because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. But buyers will also need to be aware that a dovish repricing from renewed stock market selloff could lead to more liquidations.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) probed briefly below the key 3,500 level but eventually bounced back to close the day above it. The buyers will likely step in around these levels, with a defined risk below the low, to position for a rally into the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower again to pile in for a drop into the 3,100 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. We can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, we have a resistance zone around the 3,600 level that adds confluence to the trendline. Again, the sellers will likely step in around these levels, with a defined risk above the resistance, to position for a drop into the 3,100 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

news.title: China hits back at Trump’s latest tariff threat as trade war tensions resurface
body: It looks like a trade war is back on the menu again. Just when markets thought they could afford to spend a little less time worrying about US-China tensions, we're back to the familiar exchange of threats between Washington and Beijing this week.
China's commerce ministry is hitting back at the latest US tariff proposals today, expressing firm opposition to Washington's Section 301 investigation into structural overcapacity.

As a reminder, the US is proposing additional tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners and that includes a 20% tariff on Chinese goods. In doing so, the latest proposal would bring the average effective tariff rate on Chinese goods back up to roughly 31%.
In essence, US president Trump is looking to rebuild his tariffs wall after the Supreme Court struck down earlier levies.

Now, the language from Beijing is a familiar one and something that we have seen a lot of in the past. At the end of the day, there is a difference between threatening retaliation and actually delivering it. On the latter, I'd actually pay more attention on how Beijing might look to hit back through other avenues. To put it more simply, I'm more interested as to when they will start to bring rare earth export restrictions back into the conversation.

As for markets, the timing of all this is hardly ideal. Investors are already wrestling with a rather painful tech selloff and renewed concerns about economic growth. So when you throw in another round of tariffs uncertainty into the mix, it definitely complicates the recovery effort.
